title: Read a commit graph without guessing
summary: Those ASCII lines are not decoration. Build a history with a fork, a merge and a divergence, then learn to read the shape — and the three flags that make a hairball legible.
mental_model: Time runs upwards. A line that splits is a branch point, a line that joins is a merge, and a commit with two lines entering it is a merge commit. Everything else is one commit following another.

commit.message: Work on main while alpha ran

steps.title: The default log hides the shape entirely
steps.why: A flat list gives no hint that two branches existed or that anything was merged. Every question about how history fits together needs `--graph`.
steps.expect: A straight list, with the merge indistinguishable from an ordinary commit.

steps.title: Add the graph and the labels
steps.why: `--graph --all --decorate` is the combination worth memorising: the shape, every branch (not just yours), and the names attached to each commit. Anything less and you are looking at part of the picture.
steps.expect: A fork, a merge bubble, and a second branch hanging off the merge — all labelled.

verify.label: the graph shows structure, not just a list

steps.title: Identify the merge commit
steps.why: A merge is the commit where two lines converge, and it is the only kind with two parents. `--merges` lists them; `%p` proves it by printing both parent shas.
steps.expect: One merge commit with two parents.

verify.label: the merge commit has exactly two parents

steps.title: Follow only the main line
steps.why: `--first-parent` treats each merge as a single event and never enters the merged branch. On a repository with hundreds of merges this is the difference between a readable release history and a wall of noise.
steps.expect: Five commits on the main line versus seven in total — the two alpha commits are skipped.

verify.label: first-parent history is shorter than the full history
verify.hint: each merge counts once and its branch is skipped

verify.label: …while the full history includes the merged branch's commits

steps.title: See a divergence
steps.why: feature/beta forked before main's last commit, so neither contains the other. `--left-right` marks which side each commit is on — the clearest way to answer 'what is on my branch that is not on main'.
steps.expect: One commit on each side — the definition of diverged.

verify.label: the two branches have one unique commit each

steps.title: Ordering changes what you see
steps.why: `--date-order` interleaves branches by time; `--topo-order` keeps each branch's commits together. When a graph looks tangled, topo order is usually the fix — the history did not change, only its presentation.

steps.title: Ask the questions the graph is really for
steps.why: Once you can see the shape, the useful queries are one command each: what is in this branch and not that one, where did they diverge, and which branches contain a given commit.
steps.expect: The unique commit, the fork point, and which branches hold the merge.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git log --oneline $(git merge-base main feature/beta)..feature/beta | wc -l'
verify.label: you can name exactly what a branch added since it forked

steps.title: Save the view you will use
steps.why: Nobody types the full incantation twice. Alias it, and reading history becomes a reflex rather than a chore.

verify.label: you can read the main line separately from the full history
you can identify a merge commit by its two parents
you can measure a divergence in both directions
the graph view is saved as an alias
nothing was modified — reading history never changes it

pitfalls: `--graph` without `--all` shows only the current branch's ancestry, so a branch you are looking for is simply absent rather than wrong.
Time runs upwards in git's output and downwards in most graphical tools. Check which way round you are reading before concluding anything.
A merge bubble means a merge commit exists. A fast-forwarded branch leaves no bubble at all, which is why some teams insist on `--no-ff`.
`--graph` forces topological ordering internally, so combining it with `--date-order` can still look non-chronological. That is correct, not a bug.
On a repository with hundreds of branches, `--all` is unreadable. Name the two or three branches you care about instead.
cheatsheet: the everyday view: shape, all branches, labels
the main line, merges as single events
prove a commit is a merge
which side each commit is on
group by branch / interleave by time
